messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 43
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Vignette:
Mara, a 43-year-old European American chef, had been in the middle of a busy dinner service when she first began to notice that something was seriously wrong with her body. She had gone to work as usual, moving between the stove and prep station with the muscle memory of years in professional kitchens, but over the course of that shift the sensation in her body sharpened into something she could not dismiss. What began as a vague feeling of being unwell quickly became a frightening medical crisis, the kind that made the fluorescent lights, the metallic smell of the kitchen, and the heat from the burners feel strangely distant and yet unbearably vivid at once. She remembers the event now as extreme and almost unbelievable, the sort of thing that still does not feel fully possible to her when she tries to say it out loud: her own body seemed to turn against her, and in the moment she could not make sense of how fast ordinary life had become life-threatening. The experience was so intense that when it comes back to her, it does not arrive as a simple recollection but as a full-bodied return, with every sense seeming to come back at once.

In the weeks and months afterward, Mara found that ordinary moments could suddenly become the doorway back into that experience. At work, the hiss of boiling water, the clatter of pans, or the sharp smell rising from a hot pan could catch her off guard and, for a brief instant, she would feel as if she were back in the original emergency. Sometimes she would freeze in the middle of service with the sense that the danger was happening again, or she would find herself acting as if her body were in immediate peril before she had even had time to think. Her hands might go tense over a cutting board, her breathing would change, and she would look around the kitchen with the hard, scanning vigilance of someone certain that something terrible might return without warning. Even in places that were objectively safe, she found she could not truly settle. A quiet evening at home, sitting beside her partner after dinner, was no guarantee of ease; her body remained keyed up, restless and unable to relax despite her knowing she was not in immediate danger.

Mara’s recollections of the illness were not only frightening but deeply sorrowful. When the memory surfaced, it did not come as a detached story; it arrived with a wave of grief so strong that she often had to stop whatever she was doing. She could be washing dishes, or opening the refrigerator at home, and suddenly feel the whole scene of the illness return with such force that she would have to sit down and look away. She found it hard to believe that the event had happened to her at all, as though it belonged to someone else’s life, and that strangeness itself seemed to leave her shaken. She described feeling bereaved not only by what occurred, but by the fact that the version of herself who existed before the illness seemed unreachable. Since then, she has come to believe that her body is permanently damaged and that it keeps reacting as though danger is still present even when she is safe. She also fears that she will never be able to feel normal emotions again, because so often she notices only a flat, numbed state where she expects warmth, pleasure, or ease.

Over time, Mara began to manage these experiences by narrowing her life. She numbs her feelings because anything tender or intense seems risky; rather than letting herself dwell on sadness, fear, or hope, she pushes emotions down and keeps moving. She has also started to avoid positive situations, especially anything that might make her feel happy or hopeful, because the prospect of hope feels precarious to her, almost like tempting fate. At home, this has meant turning away from plans that once would have mattered to her, including small celebrations or outings that her partner suggests. She often stays up very late, delaying sleep until exhaustion takes over, because night feels like a time when she can keep herself contained and avoid the vulnerability of lying down and being left alone with her body’s sensations and memories. Her partner has noticed that evenings now disappear into long stretches of watching television in silence or sitting at the kitchen table until the clock has moved far past midnight. At work, she still functions, but the kitchen is also the place where reminders can intrude, and she has become more guarded there, bracing herself whenever her body unexpectedly revives the fear.

By the time she sought help, Mara had reached a point where she was exhausted by the constant effort of holding herself together and by the conviction that her body could not be trusted. What finally brought her in was the realization that she was no longer living alongside the memory but organizing her days around keeping it at a distance. She wanted relief from the sudden reliving, from the sense that her body was still alarmed in safe places, and from the bleak certainty that she had been permanently changed. What she most hopes for is the possibility of feeling like herself again, even if only in small ways at first, and what she most fears is that she will remain trapped in this state of numbness, vigilance, and grief.
